items.title: Check
items.prompt: Holding n fixed, doubling the noise σ does what to the slope's standard error?
items.hint: The standard error of β̂₁ is proportional to σ.
items.explain: SE(β̂₁) ∝ σ, so doubling σ roughly doubles the standard error — the slider shows exactly this.
choices: halves it
leaves it unchanged
roughly doubles it
quadruples it

items.title: Does a great fit prove the cause?
items.prompt: You just fit the line and read off the summary. Claim: a regression with R² = 0.92 has clearly captured the causal effect of the regressor on y .
items.hint: R² measures in-sample fit. Does fit say anything about whether x is correlated with the error?
items.explain: This is the high-R²-is-causal trap . R² is only the fraction of in-sample variance the line reproduces — it says nothing about bias, omitted variables, or causation. A confounded regression (ability omitted from wage~schooling) can sit at R²≈0.9, while a perfectly unbiased causal estimate can have R²≈0.1. Boundary: R² and t-stats describe fit and noise ; a causal claim needs E[ε|x]=0, which no in-sample statistic can certify. Whenever a defence of causality cites R² or a t-stat, suspect this error.

items.title: Check
items.prompt: In β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, what does the column of 1s in X provide?
items.hint: Think about what a constant regressor estimates.
items.explain: The constant (column of 1s) lets the model estimate the intercept β₀.
choices: the slope
the intercept
the residuals
the standard errors

items.title: Is β̂ unbiased for the causal return?
items.prompt: You just computed β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. For wage on schooling it returns β̂ = 0.08 with R² = 0.31 and t = 9.2. This β̂ is unbiased for the causal return to schooling…
items.hint: The normal equations always return a number. Unbiasedness is a separate condition: E[ε|x]=0.
items.explain: This is the fit-vs-identification trap . The formula β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy mechanically produces an estimate no matter what — unbiasedness for the causal effect needs E[ε|x]=0. Unobserved ability lives in ε and correlates with schooling, so β̂ is biased upward regardless of t or R². Boundary: t and R² certify nothing about exogeneity — that gap is exactly why instrumental variables exist.
why: A big t-stat is about sampling noise, not bias — the formula (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy is exact regardless of significance.
Fit ≠ identification — this is the omitted-variable trap; R² can be high while β̂ is badly confounded.
Homoskedasticity affects only the standard errors, not whether β̂ is unbiased.
choices: …yes, because t = 9.2 is highly significant
…yes, because R² = 0.31 shows the model fits well
…only if schooling is uncorrelated with the error (e.g. unobserved ability)
…only if the errors are homoskedastic

items.title: Check
items.prompt: To halve a coefficient's standard error, you should multiply the sample size by about…
items.explain: Because SE shrinks like 1⁄√n, you need 4× the data to halve it.
choices: the same

items.title: What does 'explained' mean?
items.prompt: The inference summary reports R² = 0.36. What percent of the in-sample variance in y does the model account for? Enter a number, no % sign.
items.hint: R² is already a fraction of variance — just convert 0.36 to a percent.
items.explain: 36%. This defuses the word 'explained' : R² literally equals the fraction of sample variance reproduced in this sample — 'explained' here is statistical bookkeeping, not a causal claim. The tempting move is to hear 'explains 36% of y' as 'causes 36% of y'; that fails because R² is silent about bias. Boundary: 36% explained is fully compatible with a biased slope, and 99% is compatible with a hopelessly confounded one.

items.title: How much data to halve the SE?
items.prompt: You saw SE shrink like 1⁄√n. Starting from a sample of n = 250, by what factor must you multiply n to halve the slope's standard error? Enter the factor (a plain number).
items.hint: SE ∝ 1⁄√n, so halving SE means doubling √n. What does that do to n itself?
items.explain: This catches the linear-precision trap — assuming twice the data halves the SE. Because SE ∝ 1⁄√n, halving the SE requires doubling √n, which means multiplying n by 2² = 4. So n goes 250 → 1000. Boundary: the √n law makes precision expensive — each further halving of the SE costs another 4× in data, which is why huge samples buy ever less extra certainty.

items.title: Check
items.prompt: Under heteroskedasticity, ordinary OLS gives you…
items.hint: Heteroskedasticity is about the variance of the error, not its mean.
items.explain: Coefficients remain unbiased; only the standard errors are wrong — use robust (HC) SEs.
choices: biased coefficients and wrong SEs
unbiased coefficients but wrong SEs
everything correct
biased coefficients but correct SEs

items.title: Does heteroskedasticity bias the coefficients?
items.prompt: You just saw the residuals fan out with x. Claim: heteroskedasticity biases the OLS coefficients , so you must drop the affected observations.
items.hint: Heteroskedasticity changes the error's variance, not its mean. Which OLS property depends on the mean of the error?
items.explain: This is the heteroskedasticity-biases-coefficients trap . Heteroskedasticity is about the variance of the error, not its mean — so unbiasedness (which needs E[ε|x]=0) is untouched; β̂ stays unbiased and only the default standard errors are wrong. The tempting fix — deleting data — throws away valid information and introduces selection bias. Boundary: the right fix is robust (HC1) standard errors, which correct the inference while leaving the unbiased coefficients in place.

items.title: What does heteroskedasticity actually break?
items.prompt: Residuals fan out with x. Select all that apply: which statements about OLS under heteroskedasticity are TRUE?
items.hint: Separate what changes (the variance of the error, hence the SEs) from what doesn't (the mean of the error, hence unbiasedness).
items.explain: This re-plants the heteroskedasticity-biases-coefficients trap as a set. TRUE: β̂ stays unbiased (it needs E[ε|x]=0, untouched by non-constant variance), the classical SEs are wrong, and robust HC1 SEs repair the inference. FALSE distractors: 'β̂ becomes biased' is the central misconception — variance is not bias; and 'delete the high-variance observations' discards valid data and induces selection bias. Boundary: heteroskedasticity costs you efficiency and correct SEs, never unbiasedness.
choices: The coefficient estimates β̂ remain unbiased
The default (classical) standard errors are wrong
Robust (HC1) standard errors fix the inference
The coefficient estimates β̂ become biased
You should delete the high-variance observations to fix it

items.title: Check: source of the bias
items.prompt: An unobserved variable raises both schooling x and wages y. We regress wages on schooling by OLS. What happens as the sample grows very large?
items.hint: Endogeneity is about consistency, not sampling noise.
items.explain: Omitted-variable bias does not vanish with n. The point estimate converges to a wrong number while its SE shrinks around that wrong number — precise but inconsistent.
choices: The estimate converges to the true return to schooling
The estimate stays biased; only its standard error shrinks
The bias grows without bound
OLS becomes unbiased once n > 1000

items.title: Check: sign of the bias
items.prompt: In x = π·u + v and y = β₁·x + γ·u + η, suppose γ > 0 and π > 0. OLS will tend to…
items.hint: The asymptotic bias has the sign of γ·π.
items.explain: With γ·π > 0 the omitted u creates positive comovement between x and the error, so OLS attributes extra positive slope to x and overstates β₁.
choices: overstate β₁
understate β₁
estimate β₁ exactly
give a negative β̂₁ regardless

items.title: Check: which property is testable?
items.prompt: Which of the two IV conditions can you directly check from the observed data?
items.hint: One condition involves the unobservable error.
items.explain: Relevance (Cov(z,x) ≠ 0) is observable and testable via the first stage. Exclusion involves the unobservable error ε and must be argued from theory, not proven from data.
choices: Exclusion, by regressing y on z
Relevance, by checking that z is correlated with x
Both are fully testable
Neither can ever be examined

items.title: Check: a broken instrument
items.prompt: A proposed instrument z is strongly correlated with x but ALSO has its own direct effect on y. Using it in IV will…
items.hint: z must affect y ONLY through x.
items.explain: A direct z→y path violates the exclusion restriction, contaminating Cov(z,y). A huge first-stage F does not rescue an invalid instrument — it can make the bias more precise.
choices: still give a consistent estimate of β₁
violate exclusion and generally yield a biased estimate
only inflate the standard errors
be fine as long as the first-stage F is large

items.title: Significant first stage ⇒ good instrument?
items.prompt: You just saw that relevance is the one IV condition you can check in the data via the first stage. Claim: once the first-stage coefficient on z is statistically significant (t > 1.96), the instrument is strong enough to trust 2SLS.
items.hint: Significance answers a different question (is the coefficient distinguishable from zero?) than strength (does z move x enough to divide by safely?).
items.explain: This is the significance≠strength trap , the classic weak-instrument error. A first-stage t can clear 1.96 while the instrument is still weak: in 2SLS, strength is graded by the first-stage F on the excluded instruments (rule of thumb F ≳ 10), not by whether the coefficient beats zero. A barely-significant, low-F instrument biases 2SLS back toward OLS and wrecks the standard errors. Boundary: significance is necessary-ish but never sufficient — only a large first-stage F certifies strength.

items.title: What makes an instrument valid?
items.prompt: Z is a candidate instrument for an endogenous x. Select all that apply : which conditions MUST hold for Z to be a valid instrument?
items.hint: Two of these are the actual requirements you saw split into 'checkable' vs 'must be argued'; the others are properties students wrongly bolt on.
items.explain: This bundles the validity conditions : relevance + exclusion + exogeneity. The strong distractor is 'significant first-stage coefficient' — that is the significance≠strength trap; significance is neither necessary nor sufficient, and a significant first stage can still be a weak (low-F) instrument. Normality of Z is never required — IV/2SLS makes no distributional assumption on the instrument. Boundary: relevance is the only one you can test from data; exclusion and exogeneity are arguments you must defend, not p-values you can read off.
choices: Relevance: Z is correlated with x (Cov(z,x) ≠ 0)
Exclusion: Z affects y only through x
Exogeneity: Z is uncorrelated with the structural error ε
Z has a statistically significant first-stage coefficient
Z is normally distributed

items.title: Check: what goes into the second stage?
items.prompt: In 2SLS, the second-stage regression of y is run on…
items.hint: We want the clean part of x that z explains.
items.explain: The second stage uses x̂, the projection of x onto the instruments. Because x̂ is built only from exogenous z, it is uncorrelated with the confounder, giving a consistent β̂₁.
choices: the raw endogenous x
the fitted values x̂ from regressing x on the instruments
the instrument z directly
the residuals from the first stage

items.title: Check: why not hand-roll the SEs?
items.prompt: Why prefer IV2SLS over manually running sm.OLS(y, x̂) for the second stage?
items.hint: The point estimate matches; something else does not.
items.explain: Both give the same β̂₁, but plugging x̂ into a naive OLS understates uncertainty because it treats the generated regressor as if it were observed. IV2SLS corrects the variance.
choices: The manual coefficient is biased
The manual standard errors are wrong because they ignore that x̂ is estimated
IV2SLS uses a different, larger sample
There is no difference at all

items.title: The clean slice of x
items.prompt: In 2SLS the second stage regresses y not on the raw endogenous x, but on the ___ values x̂ that the first stage predicts from the instruments.
items.lead: 2SLS runs in two moves: regress x on the instruments, keep the predictions, then run the structural equation on those.
items.hint: It's the part of x that z explains — the clean, exogenous slice, written x̂.
items.explain: The blank is fitted (predicted) values, x̂. The misconception this defuses is 'plug the instrument z straight into the second stage' — you regress y on x̂, not on z and not on the first-stage residuals. x̂ keeps only the variation in x that z explains, stripping out the confounded part. Boundary: with one instrument and one endogenous regressor this two-stage fit numerically equals the simple IV ratio Cov(z,y)/Cov(z,x); with extra instruments it does not, which is the over-identified case.

items.title: Hand-rolled second-stage SEs
items.prompt: Claim: running the second stage by hand with sm.OLS(y, x̂) gives both the right 2SLS coefficient and the right standard errors.
items.hint: The point estimate matches; think about what x̂ being estimated (not observed) does to the uncertainty.
items.explain: This is the manual-2SLS-is-fine trap . The hand-rolled coefficient is correct, but the standard errors are wrong : sm.OLS(y, x̂) treats x̂ as if it were observed data, ignoring that x̂ was itself estimated in the first stage, so it understates the true sampling variability. Use a dedicated IV2SLS estimator, which corrects the SEs. Boundary: the bias is only in the inference (SEs, t-stats, CIs) — the β̂ from the manual route is identical, so the fix is the SE formula, not the point estimate.

items.title: Check: reading the first-stage F
items.prompt: Your first-stage F-statistic for the excluded instrument is 2.3. What is the appropriate concern?
items.hint: Compare against the rule-of-thumb threshold of about 10.
items.explain: An F well below 10 signals a weak instrument: the first stage barely moves x, so 2SLS estimates are imprecise and biased toward OLS, with unreliable standard errors.
choices: The exclusion restriction is violated
The instrument is weak; 2SLS may be biased and very imprecise
The model is over-identified
Nothing — any positive F is fine

items.title: Check: the over-ID test
items.prompt: With two instruments and one endogenous regressor, the Sargan/Hansen J test returns a very small p-value. This suggests…
items.hint: The test compares the estimates implied by different instruments.
items.explain: A small p-value rejects the null that all instruments are valid: the over-identifying instruments disagree, pointing to an exclusion violation (or misspecification). It cannot run in the just-identified case.
choices: the instruments are strong
at least one instrument likely violates the exclusion restriction
the first stage is weak
β₁ is exactly 2

items.title: First-stage F vs the rule of thumb
items.prompt: The first stage regresses x on the excluded instrument; the F-statistic on that instrument is 6.4 . Using the Staiger–Stock rule of thumb (F ≈ 10), how far above or below the threshold are you? Enter a signed number (e.g. −3.6).
items.hint: Subtract the threshold from your F: 6.4 − 10.
items.explain: 6.4 − 10 = −3.6 , i.e. 3.6 below the rule-of-thumb 10 — a weak instrument. This is the significance≠strength trap again in numbers: that same first stage could have a significant t-stat, yet an F of 6.4 means 2SLS is biased toward OLS with distorted standard errors. 'Significant' and 'strong' are different claims; only the F speaks to strength. Boundary: F ≳ 10 is a rough threshold, not a bright line — values just above it are reassuring, low single digits are a clear red flag regardless of how clean the exclusion story is.

items.title: What a passed over-ID test proves
items.prompt: Your over-identified model has 3 instruments for 1 endogenous regressor. The Sargan/Hansen J test returns a large p-value (you fail to reject). What can you correctly conclude?
items.hint: The J test can only ever reject validity; ask what failing to reject does and doesn't establish.
items.explain: This is the passed-test-proves-exogeneity trap . The over-ID (Sargan/Hansen J) test can only reject validity: a large p-value is consistent with valid instruments but proves nothing — the test has low power and must assume at least one instrument is valid to anchor on. Exclusion/exogeneity stays an argument you defend, not a result you read off. The strength distractor confuses two diagnostics: weakness is the first-stage F, validity is the J test. Boundary: the J test is also silent when the model is just-identified (one instrument, one regressor) — there are no spare instruments to disagree, so there is nothing to test.
why: The over-ID test can only reject; a non-rejection never proves validity.
That is what a SMALL p-value (rejection) would suggest, not a large one.
The J test checks exclusion/over-ID agreement, not strength — strength is the first-stage F.
choices: The exclusion restriction is now proven — all 3 instruments are valid
The result is consistent with valid instruments, but exclusion remains an untested assumption
At least one instrument violates exclusion
The instruments are strong (high first-stage F)

items.title: Check
items.prompt: A common economy-wide shock makes BOTH groups' outcomes rise by 5 between before and after. What happens to the DiD estimate?
items.hint: DiD subtracts the control group's change, which now contains that +5.
items.explain: A shock common to both groups enters both Δtreated and Δcontrol, so it cancels in the difference of differences. DiD is designed to be immune to such common shocks.
choices: It rises by 5
It rises by 10
It is unchanged
It falls by 5

items.title: The control group is a what?
items.prompt: In DiD, the control group's before-to-after change is used as an estimate of the treated group's ___ change — what would have happened to the treated units absent treatment.
items.lead: You just saw that subtracting the control group's change strips out common trends and shocks, leaving the causal effect.
items.hint: It is the change the treated group *would* have had with no policy — a word starting with 'counter'.
items.explain: The 'control is just another treated group' slip. The control group is a counterfactual machine: its change estimates the trend/shocks the treated group would also have felt, so subtracting it nets those out and leaves the treatment effect. The tempting reading — that the control is simply a second observation of the effect — fails because the control is never treated; its only job is to reveal the common trend. This holds only if that common trend really is shared (parallel trends); if the groups' trends diverge, the control is the wrong counterfactual.

items.title: Check
items.prompt: In the regression y ~ treated*post, which coefficient is the causal DiD estimate (the ATT)?
items.hint: Which coefficient survives the double difference after the others cancel?
items.explain: Only the interaction 'treated:post' captures the extra change in the treated group beyond the common trend; the other terms cancel in the difference-of-differences.
choices: The coefficient on 'treated'
The coefficient on 'post'
The coefficient on 'treated:post'
The intercept

items.title: Check
items.prompt: What does the coefficient on 'treated' (β₁) by itself represent?
items.hint: Set post = 0 and compare treated to control.
items.explain: β₁ is the baseline (before-period) difference in levels between the groups. It is a fixed gap, not an effect — DiD explicitly allows the groups to differ in levels.
choices: The treatment effect
The pre-treatment level gap between treated and control groups
The common time trend
The post-period outcome of the control group

items.title: Equal pre-treatment levels?
items.prompt: DiD requires the treated and control groups to have equal outcome levels before treatment.
items.hint: Which coefficient in y ~ treated*post absorbs a fixed before-period gap between the groups?
items.explain: The levels-vs-trends confusion. DiD allows any baseline level gap — that gap is exactly what β₁ (the 'treated' coefficient) absorbs, which is why the module called it a fixed level difference, not an effect. The tempting belief — that the groups must start equal — confuses a constant level gap (harmless, differenced away) with a difference in trends (fatal). Boundary: different starting levels are fine; differently-sloped trends break identification. Pivot word: levels (ok) vs trends (not ok).

items.title: Check
items.prompt: The treated group sits 8 points above the control group in BOTH the before and after periods, and both rise by 3 over time. Is parallel trends satisfied?
items.hint: Parallel trends concerns changes over time, not the level gap.
items.explain: A constant level gap with equal changes (both +3) means the trends are parallel. DiD allows different levels; it only needs equal trends.
choices: No, the 8-point gap violates it
Yes, the gap is constant so the trends are parallel
Cannot tell without the true ATT
No, because they are not at the same level

items.title: Check
items.prompt: If the treated group was already trending up faster than control before treatment, the standard 2×2 DiD estimate of a positive ATT will tend to be:
items.hint: The estimator mistakes the extra pre-existing growth for treatment effect.
items.explain: A positive differential pre-trend adds to the treated group's change, and DiD attributes that extra change to treatment, overstating the ATT.
choices: Unbiased
Biased upward (too large)
Biased downward (too small)
Exactly zero

items.title: Big post gap, diverging pre-trends
items.prompt: If the treated and control groups had different pre-treatment trends , the DiD estimate is still unbiased as long as the post-period gap is large.
items.hint: What does the module say the estimate equals when there is a differential trend δ per period?
items.explain: The parallel-trends-is-everything trap. Identification rests entirely on parallel counterfactual trends; diverging pre-trends are direct evidence that assumption fails, and the module showed the estimate becomes ATT̂ ≈ true ATT + (differential trend over the window). A large post gap is no defense — the seductive belief that a big effect 'swamps' the bias fails because the trend difference is baked into that gap and DiD cannot separate the two. Boundary: only when pre-trends are parallel does the control's change equal the treated counterfactual and β₃ recover the true ATT.

items.title: DiD from a 2×2 table
items.prompt: A 2×2 DiD: the treated group's mean goes 40 → 62, the control group's mean goes 38 → 45. Enter the DiD estimate (treated change minus control change), in points.
items.hint: First find each group's change, then subtract: (62−40) − (45−38).
items.explain: The 'forget the counterfactual trend' trap. (62−40) − (45−38) = 22 − 7 = 15 . The control's change of 7 is the common shock the treated group would also have felt, so subtracting it nets out the trend. The seductive wrong answer is 22 — the raw treated change — which credits the policy with the entire before/after move and ignores that part of it was just the shared trend. Boundary: 22 would be the right answer only if the control's change were 0, i.e. nothing happened to anyone absent treatment.

items.title: Check
items.prompt: In an event-study plot, what is the purpose of inspecting the PRE-treatment (lead) coefficients?
items.hint: Before treatment there can be no effect, so any nonzero value means something else is going on.
items.explain: Leads capture treated-vs-control differences before treatment, where the effect must be zero. Near-zero leads support parallel trends; nonzero leads reveal a pre-trend that invalidates the design.
choices: They measure the treatment effect
They test the parallel-trends assumption — they should be near zero
They set the reference period
They measure how fast the effect fades out

items.title: Check
items.prompt: Why is the reference period's coefficient exactly 0 with no confidence interval?
items.hint: All θₜ are differences relative to that one omitted period.
items.explain: The reference (omitted) period is the baseline against which all other coefficients are defined, so it is mechanically 0 and carries no sampling uncertainty.
choices: The effect happens to be zero there
Every other period is measured relative to it, so it is normalized to 0 by construction
Its standard error is too large to plot
Treatment has no effect in that period

items.title: Reading a significant lead
items.prompt: Your event-study plot shows a pre-treatment (lead) coefficient that is large and statistically significant, well away from zero. What does this tell you?
items.hint: Where the effect must be zero, a coefficient far from zero is bad news, not good.
items.explain: The 'significant pre-trend is reassuring' trap. Leads sit before treatment, where the true effect is zero, so they should hug zero; a large significant lead is evidence the groups were already diverging — a pre-trend that invalidates the design. The tempting belief flips the logic of a falsification test: you want to fail to reject here, not to find significance. Boundary: flat (near-zero) leads are necessary but not sufficient — failing to reject a pre-trend makes parallelism plausible, it never proves the untestable post-period counterfactual.
why: Backwards: leads should hug zero. A significant lead is evidence AGAINST parallel trends, not for the design.
Leads are before treatment, where the effect is zero by definition — they cannot measure post-treatment dynamics.
The reference period is the one normalized to 0 with no error bar; it is not the lead you are reading.
choices: It is reassuring — a significant pre-period coefficient confirms the design is working
It is a warning — a nonzero lead signals a pre-trend that undercuts parallel trends
It measures how quickly the treatment effect fades after treatment
It sets the reference period, so it should be large by construction

items.title: What the event-study plot tells you
items.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about an event-study (dynamic DiD) plot are TRUE?
items.hint: Two of the five are classic traps: one over-claims what flat leads prove, one misreads what a significant lead means.
items.explain: The 'flat leads = proven parallelism' over-claim. True: leads near zero are the visual test of parallel trends; the reference period is mechanically 0 with no error bar; lags trace the dynamic effect. False trap 1 — flat pre-period leads are necessary but not sufficient : parallel trends in the post period is untestable, since the treated counterfactual is never observed, so leads make it plausible, not proven. False trap 2 — a significant lead is the opposite of reassuring; it signals a pre-trend. Boundary: the event-study only ever offers indirect, pre-period evidence — it can falsify the design but never certify the post-period counterfactual.
choices: Pre-treatment (lead) coefficients should be near zero if parallel trends holds
The reference period's coefficient is exactly 0 by construction, with no confidence interval
Post-treatment (lag) coefficients trace how the effect turns on and evolves over time
Flat pre-period leads prove the parallel-trends assumption holds in the post period
A statistically significant lead coefficient is reassuring evidence for the design

items.title: Check: what makes it a VAR?
items.prompt: In the VAR(1) matrix A, what does a non-zero off-diagonal entry a₁₂ represent?
items.hint: Read off the first equation: y1ₜ = c₁ + a₁₁·y1ₜ₋₁ + a₁₂·y2ₜ₋₁ + ε1ₜ.
items.explain: a₁₂ multiplies the lagged value of the OTHER variable (y2ₜ₋₁) in the equation for y1, so it is the cross-variable spillover; own-persistence lives on the diagonal.
choices: The persistence of y1 (how much of its own past it keeps)
The effect of last period's y2 on this period's y1
The contemporaneous correlation of the two error terms
The long-run mean of y1

items.title: Check: stability
items.prompt: A VAR(1) is stationary (stable) when…
items.hint: It is the multivariate version of the AR(1) rule |φ| < 1.
items.explain: Stationarity depends on the eigenvalues of A, not the raw entries — a matrix with large entries can still be stable, and one with small entries can be explosive.
choices: every entry of A is less than 1 in absolute value
the determinant of A is positive
every eigenvalue of A has modulus less than 1
the off-diagonal entries are zero

items.title: Does the spillover die out?
items.prompt: A shock δ = 1 hits y1 at time 0 in a stable VAR(1) with coefficient matrix A. The horizon-2 response of the system is A²·δ. If A = [[0.5, 0.4],[0.0, 0.5]], enter the horizon-2 response of y1 (first component of A²·δ, where δ = (1, 0)′), to two decimals.
items.hint: δ = (1,0)′, so you only need the (1,1) entry of A². For this upper-triangular A that is just 0.5².
items.explain: The 'spillover never fades' trap. The horizon-h response is Aʰ·δ; here A²·δ has first component (0.5² + 0.4·0) = 0.25, down from 0.5 at horizon 1 and heading to 0. Because A is stable (both eigenvalues 0.5, modulus < 1), shocks are transitory and decay geometrically. Boundary: if any eigenvalue of A had modulus ≥ 1 the series would be non-stationary and the response would not die out — stability, not the size of the raw entries, is what guarantees decay.

items.title: Check: which criterion?
items.prompt: You care most about not overfitting and want the most parsimonious lag order that is consistent for the true p. Which criterion do you lean on?
items.hint: One of these has a penalty that grows with log(n) and is the strictest.
items.explain: BIC's penalty (∝ log n · #params) is the harshest, so it selects fewer lags and is consistent for the true order; AIC/FPE favor richer models better suited to pure forecasting.
choices: AIC
BIC (SC)
FPE
always use the maximum lag

items.title: Check: estimation method
items.prompt: Why can a VAR be estimated by running OLS separately on each equation without losing efficiency?
items.hint: Think about what SUR/GLS would buy you when all equations have identical regressors.
items.explain: When every equation has the same regressors, the GLS (SUR) estimator collapses to equation-by-equation OLS, so separate OLS is already fully efficient even though the errors are correlated across equations.
choices: Because the errors are independent across equations
Because every equation shares exactly the same set of regressors (the stacked lags)
Because OLS is always efficient
Because the residual covariance Σ is diagonal

items.title: Which criterion picks the fewest lags?
items.prompt: Among AIC, BIC, and HQIC, the criterion with the harshest penalty (∝ log n · #params) — so it selects the fewest lags and is consistent for the true order — is ___.
items.lead: select_order printed AIC, BIC, and HQIC side by side; you must name the one that penalizes extra parameters hardest.
items.hint: Its penalty grows with log n, so it punishes extra parameters harder than AIC as the sample grows.
items.explain: The all-criteria-agree assumption. BIC (a.k.a. SC / Schwarz) carries the heaviest penalty (∝ log n per parameter), so it selects fewer lags and is consistent for the true lag order. AIC and FPE use a lighter, fixed penalty and tend to pick more lags — better for pure forecasting, not for recovering the true order. Boundary: when the goal is forecasting rather than identifying the true p, the richer AIC model can legitimately win, so the criteria need not, and often do not, agree.

items.title: Check: ordering matters
items.prompt: You compute orthogonalized IRFs, then swap the order of the two columns in your DataFrame and recompute. What can change?
items.hint: Cholesky imposes a recursive timing assumption based on column order.
items.explain: Orthogonalization via Cholesky assumes earlier-ordered variables can hit later ones contemporaneously but not the reverse; changing the order changes that assumption and hence the impact responses.
choices: Nothing — orthogonalization is order-invariant
The contemporaneous (impact) responses, because the Cholesky ordering changes which variable can affect the other within the same period
Only the long-run responses
The estimated coefficient matrix A

items.title: Check: reading FEVD
items.prompt: A FEVD says that at horizon 10, 85% of y1's forecast-error variance comes from its own shock and 15% from the y2 shock. This means…
items.hint: FEVD shares are about variance attribution, and they sum to 1 across shocks for each variable.
items.explain: FEVD splits a variable's forecast uncertainty into shares per shock; 85% own-share means y1's unpredictability is mostly self-generated at horizon 10, with y2 contributing only 15%.
choices: y1 is mostly driven by its own innovations at that horizon
y2 Granger-causes y1 with p < 0.15
the IRF of y1 to a y2 shock is exactly 0.15
y1 and y2 are uncorrelated

items.title: Significant VAR coefficient: what does it prove?
items.prompt: In your fitted reduced-form VAR, the lagged-X coefficient in the Y equation is large and highly significant, and the orthogonalized IRF of Y to an X shock is clearly non-zero. The safest reading is:
items.hint: A reduced-form VAR is silent about structure until you impose an assumption.
items.explain: The reduced-form-significance-is-structural trap. A significant lag coefficient (or a non-zero orthogonalized IRF) is predictive precedence — exactly Granger content — not a verified structural effect. The orthogonalized IRF only looks structural because you supplied a Cholesky ordering ; reorder the variables and the impact responses move. Boundary: the structural reading is valid only when the ordering's contemporaneous-causal assumption is itself defensible, which the data cannot confirm.
why: Significance is reduced-form predictive content, not proof of a structural mechanism.
Reordering changes which variable can hit the other contemporaneously, so impact responses do change.
orth_irfs imposes an ordering you chose; that choice IS the identifying assumption, it is not automatic.
choices: X structurally causes Y — the significant coefficient settles it
Past X carries predictive information about Y; calling it a structural effect needs an imposed identification (the ordering)
Reordering the Cholesky variables would leave the impact responses unchanged
The IRF is structural automatically because it came from orth_irfs

items.title: Are IRFs structural for free?
items.prompt: Claim: you can read structural impulse responses straight off a reduced-form VAR with no identifying assumption — orth_irfs just returns them.
items.hint: What did you have to choose before the Cholesky factor was even defined?
items.explain: The IRFs-are-structural-for-free trap. Orthogonalized IRFs require a Cholesky factor of Σ, and that factor depends on a variable ordering you impose : the earlier variable may hit the later one contemporaneously but not vice versa. Reorder the columns and the impact responses change — so the structure came from your assumption, not the data. Boundary: the reduced-form VAR alone pins down forecasts and correlations; turning those into structural shocks always needs an extra identifying restriction (ordering, sign restrictions, or external instruments).

items.title: Check: what Granger causality is (and isn't)
items.prompt: A test finds that y2 Granger-causes y1 (p = 0.001). The safest interpretation is:
items.hint: The name is misleading; it is fundamentally a statement about forecasting.
items.explain: Granger causality only certifies predictive content of y2's history for y1; it does not establish structural causation, allows correlation, and is not exclusive (causality can run both ways).
choices: Changing y2 will mechanically change y1 — true causation is proven
Past values of y2 improve forecasts of y1 beyond y1's own past
y1 and y2 must be contemporaneously uncorrelated
y1 cannot also Granger-cause y2

items.title: Check: forecast bands
items.prompt: As the forecast horizon h grows, the width of a VAR's forecast interval typically…
items.hint: For a stable VAR, the forecast converges to the mean and the forecast-error variance converges to a finite limit.
items.explain: Forecast-error variance accumulates with horizon but, because the VAR is stationary, it converges to the series' unconditional variance, so the bands widen and then flatten rather than growing forever.
choices: shrinks toward zero
stays constant
widens and then levels off at the stationary (unconditional) variance
oscillates without bound

items.title: Does Granger causality mean causation?
items.prompt: You just ran the block F-test and found that X Granger-causes Y (p = 0.001). Claim: this proves that X causes Y — intervening on X would move Y.
items.hint: Read the name literally as a forecasting statement, not a philosophical one.
items.explain: The Granger-is-causation trap. Granger causality only says past X improves the forecast of Y beyond Y's own past — it is predictive precedence, not structural cause. A common driver or anticipation (X is a leading indicator) yields Granger causality with no causal link from X to Y. Boundary: a structural causal claim needs an identifying assumption you impose (e.g. a Cholesky ordering); no in-sample F-test can supply it.

items.title: What's true about a reduced-form VAR?
items.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about a reduced-form VAR are TRUE?
items.hint: Two of these are the headline VAR traps — a significant coefficient is predictive, and more lags is not free.
items.explain: Two traps are bundled here. TRUE: Granger = predictive precedence; orthogonalized IRFs hinge on the ordering you impose; a level VAR on unit-root series can manufacture spurious dynamics (difference or use a VECM if cointegrated). FALSE: a significant coefficient is reduced-form prediction, never structural proof — the structural-from-significance trap; and 'more lags is always safer' burns degrees of freedom (a k-variable VAR(p) has k·(k·p+1) parameters) and overfits. Boundary: more lags only helps when residual autocorrelation says you genuinely under-fit; otherwise an information criterion like BIC trims it back.
choices: Granger causality means predictive precedence, not structural causation
Cholesky-orthogonalized impulse responses depend on the variable ordering you impose
Estimating in non-stationary levels can read spurious dynamics as real
A statistically significant lag coefficient proves X structurally causes Y
Adding more lags is always the safer choice

items.title: Check: what is αᵢ?
items.prompt: In yᵢₜ = β₀ + β₁·xᵢₜ + αᵢ + εᵢₜ, what distinguishes αᵢ from εᵢₜ?
items.hint: The 'i' subscript with no 't' is the giveaway.
items.explain: αᵢ carries only an i subscript, so it is fixed across all periods of entity i but differs from entity to entity. εᵢₜ carries both subscripts and is the usual time-varying noise. Both are unobserved.
choices: αᵢ varies over time within an entity; εᵢₜ is constant
αᵢ is constant within an entity but differs across entities; εᵢₜ varies over both i and t
αᵢ is observed in the data; εᵢₜ is unobserved
They are identical; the notation is redundant

items.title: Check: when does αᵢ cause bias?
items.prompt: A naive regression of y on x (ignoring αᵢ) gives a biased β₁ precisely when:
items.hint: Bias comes from correlation between the regressor and the omitted term.
items.explain: Bias arises from omitted-variable correlation: if x is correlated with the omitted αᵢ, the slope absorbs αᵢ's effect. A large but uncorrelated αᵢ only inflates variance, it does not bias the slope.
choices: αᵢ has large variance
T is small
Cov(xᵢₜ, αᵢ) ≠ 0
εᵢₜ is heteroskedastic

items.title: Name the hidden entity effect
items.prompt: The time-invariant, entity-specific term αᵢ that you cannot observe — a firm's culture, a person's innate ability — is called the unobserved ___ effect, and it is what biases naive regression when it moves with x.
items.lead: You just saw each entity sit at its own height αᵢ, a fixed trait carried in every one of its observations.
items.hint: It is the word for entities differing in fixed, unmeasured ways — not 'error', not 'noise'.
items.explain: The αᵢ-is-just-noise trap. αᵢ is unobserved heterogeneity : a fixed entity trait, not random scatter. The tempting belief that it is ordinary error fails because error averages to zero and is uncorrelated with x, whereas αᵢ is a persistent level that can correlate with x — that correlation, not its mere presence, is what biases a naive regression. Boundary: if Cov(x, αᵢ)=0 the heterogeneity is harmless to consistency (RE territory); only correlated heterogeneity demands the within transform.

items.title: Check: direction of the bias
items.prompt: You set the slider so α loads NEGATIVELY onto x (loading ≈ −1.5). What happens to the pooled slope relative to the true value of 2?
items.hint: Bias direction follows the sign of Cov(x, α).
items.explain: A negative loading makes Cov(x, α) < 0, so high-x entities sit lower (low α). That flattens the apparent slope, pulling pooled OLS below the true value of 2.
choices: It stays at 2 — the sign of the loading doesn't matter
It is biased upward (above 2)
It is biased downward (below 2)
It becomes exactly 0

items.title: Pooled OLS: inefficient, or worse?
items.prompt: When the entity effect αᵢ is correlated with the regressor, pooled OLS is not merely inefficient — its slope estimate β̂₁ is ___ and inconsistent.
items.lead: You watched the pooled line tilt too steeply because high-x entities also sit at high αᵢ.
items.hint: Inconsistency is the large-sample word; what is the finite-sample word for an estimate that is centered off-target?
items.explain: The 'pooled OLS is just inefficient' trap. Correlated αᵢ is textbook omitted-variable bias, so β̂₁ is biased AND inconsistent — wrong in finite samples and still wrong as n→∞. The tempting belief that pooling only costs precision fails because the omitted αᵢ sits in the error and shares variation with x, tilting the slope. Boundary: if αᵢ were uncorrelated with x, pooled OLS would be merely inefficient (not biased) — efficiency loss only, which is exactly the RE case.

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Fixed effects: within transformation & entity dummies
items.title: Check: why no constant?
items.prompt: After the within transformation (yᵢₜ − ȳᵢ) on (xᵢₜ − x̄ᵢ), why do we run OLS WITHOUT an intercept?
items.hint: What is the mean of a demeaned variable?
items.explain: Subtracting each entity's mean makes the overall mean of both demeaned variables exactly zero, so any fitted intercept would be zero. We drop it (and the dummy method already fits per-entity intercepts that play that role).
choices: An intercept would reintroduce αᵢ
Demeaning forces both variables to have mean zero, so the intercept is identically zero
statsmodels does not allow intercepts in panel models
To save a degree of freedom for the slope

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Fixed effects: within transformation & entity dummies
items.title: Check: what FE cannot estimate
items.prompt: Your panel includes a regressor 'female' that never changes within a person. What does the fixed-effects (within) estimator do with its coefficient?
items.hint: Demean a variable that is constant within an entity — what's left?
items.explain: A within-entity-constant variable becomes all zeros after demeaning, so FE has no variation to estimate its coefficient. This is FE's main limitation; random effects (Module 4) can recover such coefficients if its assumption holds.
choices: Estimates it precisely
Cannot estimate it — demeaning wipes out any time-invariant regressor
Estimates it but with the wrong sign
Uses it as the entity effect

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Fixed effects: within transformation & entity dummies
items.title: Name the transformation
items.prompt: The estimator that removes time-invariant unit confounders by subtracting each entity's own time-mean from every observation is the ___ (fixed-effects) estimator.
items.lead: You just derived (yᵢₜ − ȳᵢ) = β₁·(xᵢₜ − x̄ᵢ) + (εᵢₜ − ε̄ᵢ): demeaning made αᵢ − αᵢ = 0 vanish.
items.hint: It uses only the variation of x around each entity's own mean — its mirror image, the 'between' estimator, uses cross-entity means.
items.explain: The within-vs-between mix-up. The within estimator demeans each entity, sweeping out everything constant per entity — including αᵢ — and so identifies β₁ from within-entity variation alone. The tempting confusion with the BETWEEN estimator fails because between uses only cross-entity means, the very channel αᵢ contaminates, so it cannot purge the heterogeneity. Boundary: within buys consistency but discards all between-entity (time-invariant) information, so any regressor constant within an entity is wiped out and unidentified.

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Fixed effects: within transformation & entity dummies
items.title: Can FE price a fixed trait?
items.prompt: Because fixed effects is the consistent estimator under correlated αᵢ, it can also recover the coefficient on a time-invariant regressor such as a person's gender.
items.hint: The within transform subtracts each entity's mean — what happens to a variable that never changes within an entity?
items.explain: The 'FE estimates everything' trap. FE is consistent under correlated αᵢ, but the within demeaning that buys that consistency also subtracts off any variable constant within an entity — a time-invariant regressor becomes all zeros and drops out, so its coefficient is unidentified . The tempting belief fails on this exact margin: consistency for x is bought by discarding between-entity information, and a time-invariant trait lives entirely in that discarded between part. Boundary: to price a time-invariant regressor you need RE (or pooled OLS), which retains between-entity variation — at the cost of assuming Cov(x, αᵢ)=0.

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Fixed effects: within transformation & entity dummies
items.title: Smaller SEs, so use RE?
items.prompt: You just confirmed fixed effects sweeps αᵢ away and stays consistent under correlated αᵢ. Even so, since random effects yields smaller standard errors, RE is the better estimator to report here.
items.hint: RE's smaller standard errors are only meaningful if RE is centered on the truth — is it, when αᵢ correlates with x?
items.explain: The efficiency-over-consistency trap, the central FE-vs-RE error. Under correlated αᵢ, RE is inconsistent , so its smaller standard errors describe a tight interval around the wrong value — consistency must come before efficiency. The seductive 'smaller SEs win' rule fails because precision is only a virtue once the estimator is centered on the truth, and demeaning is what guarantees that here. Boundary: RE's efficiency genuinely wins when Cov(x, αᵢ)=0 (Hausman fails to reject), where both estimators are consistent and RE is simply tighter.

items.moduleTitle: 4 · Random effects & choosing FE vs RE
items.title: Check: reading the Hausman result
items.prompt: A Hausman test returns a large statistic (p-value ≈ 0.001), meaning FE and RE estimates differ sharply. What should you conclude?
items.hint: A big gap means RE's zero-correlation assumption is failing.
items.explain: A large Hausman statistic signals the estimators disagree, which happens when Cov(x, α) ≠ 0 and RE is inconsistent. You reject RE and rely on the always-consistent fixed-effects estimator.
choices: RE is fine and more efficient — keep RE
Reject RE; αᵢ is correlated with x, so use fixed effects
Both estimators are biased; use pooled OLS
Increase T and re-run RE

items.moduleTitle: 4 · Random effects & choosing FE vs RE
items.title: Check: when RE wins
items.prompt: You need the effect of a time-invariant regressor (e.g. a person's birth region) AND a Hausman test does not reject RE. Which estimator do you use?
items.hint: FE demeans away time-invariant variables; RE does not.
items.explain: When Hausman does not reject (αᵢ ⟂ x), RE is consistent and efficient, and crucially it retains time-invariant regressors that FE would wipe out — so RE is the right choice.
choices: Fixed effects — it is always safest
Random effects — it is consistent here and, unlike FE, can estimate time-invariant regressors
Pooled OLS — it ignores αᵢ
Neither is identified

items.moduleTitle: 4 · Random effects & choosing FE vs RE
items.title: Hausman rejects RE — now what?
items.prompt: Your panel has plausibly Cov(x, αᵢ) ≠ 0, and the Hausman test returns a large statistic (p = 0.002), so β̂_FE and β̂_RE disagree sharply. Which estimator should you report for β₁?
items.hint: A large Hausman statistic means the two estimators disagree — which one is the one that survives correlated αᵢ?
items.explain: The efficiency-over-consistency trap, the central FE-vs-RE error. A large Hausman statistic rejects RE's Cov(x, αᵢ)=0 assumption, so RE is inconsistent here and you report fixed effects , which demeans αᵢ away regardless of correlation. The seductive belief 'RE has smaller standard errors, so prefer it' fails because efficiency is worthless around a biased center — a tight interval on the wrong number. Boundary: RE's efficiency is real and decisive ONLY when Hausman fails to reject (small statistic), i.e. when αᵢ truly is uncorrelated with x.
why: The efficiency-over-consistency trap: smaller SEs around a biased center are worthless.
Backwards — a large Hausman statistic REJECTS RE's assumption, it does not confirm it.
Pooled OLS is the most biased here; using more variation includes the contaminated between-entity part.
choices: Random effects, because it is more efficient (smaller standard errors)
Random effects, because the Hausman test confirms its assumption holds
Fixed effects, because it stays consistent whether or not αᵢ correlates with x
Pooled OLS, because it uses all the variation in the data

items.moduleTitle: 4 · Random effects & choosing FE vs RE
items.title: RE by default?
items.prompt: Random effects is more efficient than fixed effects, so you should prefer random effects by default.
items.hint: Efficiency is a property RE only has WHEN one assumption holds — what is that assumption, and is it usually safe in economics?
items.explain: The efficiency-over-consistency trap. RE is more efficient, but only IF Cov(x, αᵢ)=0; when αᵢ correlates with x — the usual reason you reached for panel data — RE is inconsistent , and consistency must come before efficiency. The tempting 'smaller SEs win' rule fails because a precise estimate centered on the wrong value is worse than an imprecise unbiased one; the Hausman test adjudicates exactly this. Boundary: 'default to RE' is sound only after Hausman fails to reject, or when you specifically need a time-invariant coefficient FE cannot deliver.

items.moduleTitle: 1 · Why a linear model fails for 0/1 outcomes
items.title: Check
items.prompt: Which problem is NOT a structural flaw of the Linear Probability Model for a 0/1 outcome?
items.hint: Think about how the LPM is actually fit versus what logit/probit require.
items.explain: The LPM is fit by ordinary least squares — that is its whole appeal. The genuine flaws are out-of-range predictions, built-in heteroskedasticity, and a constant (rather than diminishing) marginal effect.
choices: Fitted probabilities can fall below 0 or above 1
The error variance p(1−p) depends on x, so errors are heteroskedastic
It forces a constant marginal effect of x at every probability level
It can only be estimated by maximum likelihood, never by OLS

items.moduleTitle: 1 · Why a linear model fails for 0/1 outcomes
items.title: Check
items.prompt: Why should the effect of x on P(y=1) shrink as the probability approaches 0 or 1?
items.hint: You cannot push a probability above 1.
items.explain: Near the floor or ceiling there is almost no room left, so the same change in x can only nudge the probability a tiny amount — implying an S-shaped curve, not a straight line.
choices: Because the sample size falls at the extremes
Because a probability is bounded in [0,1], so there is little room left to move
Because OLS standard errors grow at the extremes
Because x stops varying at the extremes

items.moduleTitle: 1 · Why a linear model fails for 0/1 outcomes
items.title: Does a straight line have a constant effect?
items.prompt: You just saw the Linear Probability Model fit a straight line to a 0/1 outcome. Claim: because the line is straight, a one-unit rise in x changes P(y=1) by the same amount whether you start at p=0.05 or at p=0.95.
items.hint: A straight line has one slope everywhere — that is the whole point of the module. Is that constant effect realistic near the 0 and 1 boundaries?
items.explain: This is the constant-marginal-effect flaw of the LPM. The claim is literally TRUE of the straight line — its slope is the same everywhere — and that is exactly why the LPM is wrong for probabilities: near p=0.95 there is almost no room left to move, so a real effect must shrink at the extremes. The fix is an S-curve (logit/probit) whose slope flattens in the tails. Boundary: a constant effect is only defensible over a narrow middle range where the fitted probabilities stay far from 0 and 1.

items.title: Check
items.prompt: In a logit model, a one-unit increase in x₁ (holding others fixed) does exactly what?
items.hint: What is the inverse of the logistic link?
items.explain: The logit link makes log[p/(1−p)] = β₀+β₁x linear, so a unit rise in x₁ adds exactly β₁ to the log-odds (adding β₁ to the normal z-score is the probit statement, not logit).
choices: Adds β₁ to the probability P(y=1)
Adds β₁ to the log-odds of y=1
Multiplies the probability by β₁
Adds β₁ to the normal z-score Φ⁻¹(p)

items.title: Check
items.prompt: You fit the same data with logit and probit. What do you expect?
items.hint: The logistic and normal CDFs have different variances but similar S-shapes.
items.explain: Because the logistic and normal links have different scales, logit coefficients run about 1.6–1.8 times the probit ones, yet the predicted probabilities and overall fit are almost indistinguishable.
choices: Identical coefficients and identical fitted probabilities
Very different fitted probabilities but identical coefficients
Coefficients differing by a roughly constant scale, with nearly identical fitted probabilities
Probit coefficients exactly double the logit coefficients

items.title: Is the coefficient a probability change?
items.prompt: You just fit the logit and read β̂₁ off the summary, with log[p/(1−p)] = β₀ + β₁x. Claim: β̂₁ is the change in the probability P(y=1) for a one-unit rise in x.
items.hint: Look at what the link makes linear. β multiplies x on the log-odds scale, not on the probability scale.
items.explain: This is the coefficient-is-a-marginal-effect trap, the central logit error. β is a constant change in the log-odds , not the probability: log[p/(1−p)] = β₀+β₁x is what's linear in x. The effect on the probability is β·p(1−p) — non-linear, largest near p=0.5 and tiny in the tails — so it has no single value. Boundary: only on the log-odds scale is the effect a constant β; on the probability scale you must compute an (average) marginal effect.

items.title: What does the logit make linear?
items.prompt: The logit's special trick: it makes the ___ a linear function β₀+β₁x of the regressors.
items.lead: The logistic link is chosen precisely because one transformation of the probability comes out linear in x — name that quantity.
items.hint: It is the natural log of p/(1−p). Two words, hyphenated — or the one-word name of the link itself.
items.explain: The logit (log-odds) is what comes out linear: log[p/(1−p)] = β₀+β₁x. Students often answer 'probability' or 'odds', but neither is linear in x — only the log of the odds is, which is exactly why β adds to the log-odds and not to p. Boundary: exponentiate once and you get the odds (multiplied by e^β); the probability itself is the non-linear S-curve and is never linear in x.

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Interpreting coefficients: odds ratios & marginal effects
items.title: Check
items.prompt: A logit gives a coefficient of 0.69 on x₁. What is the cleanest one-line interpretation?
items.hint: Exponentiate the coefficient.
items.explain: e^0.69 ≈ 2, so the odds (not the probability) are multiplied by about 2 — the odds ratio is the constant, exponentiated read of a logit coefficient.
choices: A one-unit rise in x₁ raises P(y=1) by 0.69
A one-unit rise in x₁ roughly doubles the odds of y=1, since e^0.69≈2
A one-unit rise in x₁ doubles the probability of y=1
x₁ explains 69% of the variation in y

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Interpreting coefficients: odds ratios & marginal effects
items.title: Check
items.prompt: Why is the average marginal effect (dP/dx) usually smaller than coefficient/4?
items.hint: Where on the S-curve is p·(1−p) largest?
items.explain: The factor p·(1−p) peaks at 0.25 when p=0.5, giving the divide-by-4 maximum; observations in the flatter tails contribute smaller slopes, pulling the average below that peak.
choices: Because statsmodels uses robust standard errors
Because coefficient/4 is the maximum effect, reached only at p=0.5, and most observations sit away from there
Because marginal effects ignore the intercept
Because the AME is measured in odds, not probability

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Interpreting coefficients: odds ratios & marginal effects
items.title: Turn the coefficient into an odds ratio
items.prompt: A logit gives a coefficient of 0.69 on treated . The odds ratio is exp(β). Enter exp(0.69) to two decimals (a plain number, no units).
items.hint: exp(0.69) is just under 2. This multiplies the ODDS — it is not a change in probability.
items.explain: exp(0.69) = 1.99 ≈ 2.00 — treatment roughly DOUBLES the odds. This is the odds-ratio reading of a logit coefficient, and it is constant across x. It is NOT a doubling of the probability and NOT the marginal effect on P(y=1): odds and probability move together only when p is small. Boundary: the odds ratio e^β is the one effect measure that does stay constant; the probability effect β·p(1−p) does not.

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Interpreting coefficients: odds ratios & marginal effects
items.title: The marginal effect at p = 0.5
items.prompt: A logit gives β=0.8 on a binary treatment. At a baseline probability p=0.5, the marginal effect on P(y=1) is β·p(1−p). Enter it to two decimals (a probability change, e.g. 0.20).
items.hint: Plug in: 0.8 × 0.5 × (1−0.5). The answer is a quarter of β here, not β itself.
items.explain: This is the coefficient-is-a-marginal-effect trap in numbers: the marginal effect is β·p(1−p) = 0.8·0.25 = 0.20, NOT the coefficient 0.8. And it shrinks toward the tails — at p=0.9 it is only 0.8·0.09 = 0.072. That p-dependence is exactly why you cannot read a logit coefficient as a single, constant change in probability. Boundary: p(1−p) peaks at 0.25 (p=0.5), so β/4 is the largest the marginal effect can ever be; everywhere else it is smaller.

items.moduleTitle: 3 · Interpreting coefficients: odds ratios & marginal effects
items.title: Reading a logit coefficient — select all
items.prompt: A logit reports β=0.69 on treated . Select all that apply — which statements are correct readings of this coefficient?
items.hint: Two correct statements live on the log-odds/odds scale; one more is about how the probability effect varies. The two probability-as-constant statements are the trap.
items.explain: Correct readings: β adds to the log-odds (0), the odds are multiplied by e^β ≈ 2 (1), and the probability effect varies with the baseline p, peaking near p=0.5 (4). The two distractors are the coefficient-is-a-marginal-effect trap: β is NOT a 0.69 jump in probability (2) and NOT a constant dP/dx (3) — the probability effect is β·p(1−p), which changes along the S-curve. Boundary: only the log-odds increment and the odds ratio e^β are constant; any probability statement must name the p at which it is evaluated.
choices: It adds 0.69 to the log-odds of y=1 for a one-unit change in treated
The odds of y=1 are multiplied by about 2 (e^0.69 ≈ 2)
It raises the probability P(y=1) by 0.69
It is the marginal effect dP/dx, the same at every value of x
The effect on probability depends on the baseline p, peaking near p=0.5

items.title: Check
items.prompt: A dataset is 95% zeros. A model that predicts 0 for everyone reports 95% accuracy. What does that reveal?
items.hint: How many true positives did that model catch?
items.explain: It catches zero positives despite 95% accuracy, so accuracy is uninformative under imbalance — threshold-free measures like the ROC/AUC and the true-positive rate expose the failure.
choices: The model is excellent
Accuracy alone is misleading under class imbalance; check FN/TPR and AUC
Accuracy should always be replaced by pseudo-R²
The threshold must have been set above 0.95

items.title: Check
items.prompt: An ROC AUC of 0.5 means:
items.hint: AUC is the probability a random positive outscores a random negative.
items.explain: AUC = 0.5 is the diagonal of the ROC plot — the model's probability ranking is no better than a coin flip, regardless of the chosen threshold.
choices: The model classifies everything perfectly
The model ranks positives above negatives no better than random chance
Exactly half the predictions are correct
The threshold is set to 0.5

items.title: Check
items.prompt: Raising the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 will generally:
items.hint: A higher bar to predict '1' makes the model more cautious about positives.
items.explain: Demanding p̂ ≥ 0.8 makes positive predictions rarer, so false positives fall while genuine positives get missed more often, raising false negatives — the classic precision/recall trade-off.
choices: Increase both false positives and false negatives
Decrease false positives but increase false negatives
Decrease both error types simultaneously
Leave the confusion matrix unchanged

items.title: Does 95% accuracy mean a good model?
items.prompt: A dataset is 95% zeros. You just saw that always predicting 0 scores 95% accuracy. Claim: that 95% accuracy shows the classifier is performing well.
items.hint: How many actual positives does the all-zeros rule catch? Think about the true-positive rate and the AUC, not raw accuracy.
items.explain: This is the accuracy-under-imbalance trap. A model that predicts 0 for everyone catches ZERO positives yet still scores 95% — accuracy just echoes the base rate when classes are imbalanced. Judge such a model by threshold-free, ranking measures: the true-positive rate and the ROC AUC (0.5 = no better than chance here). Boundary: accuracy is informative only when the classes are roughly balanced and the costs of the two error types are similar; otherwise lean on AUC, precision/recall, or a cost-weighted threshold.

items.title: Check: counting moments
items.prompt: You have a model with 2 parameters and you write down 5 moment conditions. This model is:
items.hint: Compare m (number of moments) with k (number of parameters).
items.explain: With m = 5 moments and k = 2 parameters, m > k: the model is over-identified. You generally can't zero out all moments at once, so GMM minimizes ḡ′Wḡ and the choice of W changes the estimate.
choices: under-identified, so GMM cannot be used
just-identified, so the weighting matrix is irrelevant
over-identified, so GMM minimizes a weighted sum of moments and W matters
exactly-identified only if the moments are independent

items.title: Check: what is a moment condition?
items.prompt: The moment condition E[x − μ] = 0 is used to estimate μ. What does the sample analog (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ̂) = 0 give you?
items.hint: Solve (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ̂) = 0 for μ̂.
items.explain: Setting the sample moment to zero gives Σxᵢ = nμ̂, i.e. μ̂ = x̄. The method-of-moments estimator of the mean is just the sample average.
choices: the sample variance
the sample mean x̄
the median of x
an arbitrary value depending on W

items.title: Counting the surplus
items.prompt: When you write down more moment conditions than parameters (m > k), the model is said to be ___.
items.lead: You just saw a model with 5 moment conditions for 2 parameters — there are more equations than unknowns.
items.hint: It's the opposite of 'just-identified' (m = k). The prefix means you have a surplus.
items.explain: The 'extra moments are wasted' instinct, named: a model with m > k is over-identified , and those surplus moments are not wasted — they give you a testable restriction (the J-test) and, if valid, extra efficiency. The tempting belief is that you should always reduce to m = k so every moment binds exactly; that throws away the over-identifying information. Boundary: exactly m = k is just-identified (moments hit zero exactly, W is irrelevant); m < k is under-identified and not estimable.

items.title: How many over-identifying restrictions?
items.prompt: A GMM model has m = 5 moment conditions and k = 2 parameters. How many over-identifying restrictions does it have? (enter a whole number)
items.hint: Over-identifying restrictions = surplus moments = m − k.
items.explain: The 'restrictions = number of moments' trap: the count of over-identifying restrictions is m − k = 5 − 2 = 3 , not 5. The tempting answer 5 counts all moments; but k of them are 'spent' pinning down the k parameters, leaving only m − k as independent checks. Boundary: when m = k the count is 0 — a just-identified model has nothing left over to test, which is exactly why no J-test exists there.

items.title: Check: which moment defines IV?
items.prompt: What moment condition does instrumental-variables estimation impose to identify β?
items.hint: OLS assumes the first one and fails when x is endogenous. IV replaces x with a variable assumed exogenous.
items.explain: IV's identifying moment is E[z·ε] = 0: the instrument is uncorrelated with the error. (We also need E[z·x] ≠ 0 — relevance — but that is the opposite of choice 4.)
choices: E[x · ε] = 0 (regressor orthogonal to error)
E[z · ε] = 0 (instrument orthogonal to error)
E[ε²] = σ² (homoskedasticity)
E[z · x] = 0 (instrument orthogonal to regressor)

items.title: Check: just-identified weighting
items.prompt: In the just-identified IV case (one instrument per endogenous regressor), changing the GMM weighting matrix W:
items.hint: Think about the value of ḡ′Wḡ at the solution when ḡ can be driven to exactly 0.
items.explain: When m = k, β̂ = (Z′X)⁻¹Z′y makes ḡ(β̂) = 0 exactly, so ḡ′Wḡ = 0 for ANY W. The weighting matrix only matters once you are over-identified.
choices: changes the estimate a lot
has no effect, because the sample moment is set exactly to zero
is required to make the estimator consistent
only matters if the errors are heteroskedastic

items.title: Just-identified GMM has another name
items.prompt: A just-identified GMM estimator (one moment per parameter, m = k) is numerically identical to the classic ___ estimator.
items.lead: You just solved Z′(y − Xβ̂) = 0 exactly and recovered β̂ = (Z′X)⁻¹Z′y — a name you already know.
items.hint: It's the estimator from the previous unit that fixes endogeneity with an exogenous z.
items.explain: The 'GMM is a brand-new method' trap: just-identified GMM = IV (and 2SLS in the linear case). The seductive belief is that GMM's machinery — the weight matrix W — always does something; but when m = k the moments hit zero exactly, so W cancels out and you get plain IV. Boundary: W only matters, and GMM only improves on IV, when you are over -identified (m > k) with extra valid moments. This is also why OLS and IV are GMM special cases, not rival methods.

items.title: Check: degrees of freedom
items.prompt: You estimate a model with 4 instruments (including the constant) and 2 parameters. The J-statistic has how many degrees of freedom?
items.hint: df = number of over-identifying restrictions = m − k.
items.explain: df = m − k = 4 − 2 = 2. There are two surplus moment conditions, so J ~ χ²(2) under the null that all instruments are valid.

items.title: Check: interpreting a small p-value
items.prompt: Your J-test returns p = 0.002. What is the right conclusion?
items.hint: A small p-value means the over-identifying restrictions are rejected.
items.explain: p = 0.002 rejects the joint null that all moments hold. Something in the instrument set is invalid (or the model is misspecified) — though the test does not tell you which instrument.
choices: All instruments are confirmed valid
Reject the null: at least one moment condition appears violated, so some instrument is likely invalid
The model is just-identified
The slope estimate must be biased upward

items.title: Does passing the J-test prove validity?
items.prompt: Your Hansen J-test returns a large p-value (you fail to reject). This proves your moment conditions are all valid.
items.hint: Think about what a non-rejection can and cannot establish — and what the test must assume to even run.
items.explain: The J-test-proves-validity trap. Failing to reject is necessary but not sufficient : the test has low power against small violations, it must assume at least one valid moment to anchor the comparison, and adding weak instruments dilutes it toward non-rejection. So a high p-value is weak evidence, never proof, of exogeneity. Correct rule: the J-test checks mutual consistency of the moments, not their joint truth. Boundary: a rejection (small p) is informative — it tells you at least one moment is invalid — but a non-rejection leaves you exactly where you started: arguing exclusion/exogeneity on theory, not on the test.

items.title: What over-identification actually buys
items.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about an over-identified GMM model (m > k, all reasoning about valid vs invalid moments) are TRUE?
items.hint: Four of these are textbook-true. The false one is the 'more is always better' slogan — think about what instrument proliferation does in finite samples.
items.explain: The 'more moments always reduce bias' trap is the lone false choice. Over-ID is what enables the J-test; extra valid moments buy efficiency; a rejected J flags an invalid moment (rethink or drop it, don't pile on more); and just-identified GMM = IV. The slogan that fails: instrument proliferation worsens finite-sample bias (the estimator drifts toward OLS) and weakens the J-test's power. Boundary: the efficiency gain holds asymptotically and only for valid moments; in finite samples each extra instrument also adds noise, so quantity is not free.
choices: Over-identification is what makes the J / Hansen test possible at all
Extra moment conditions improve efficiency — but only if they are valid
A rejected J-test signals that at least one moment condition is invalid
Just-identified GMM (m = k) coincides with the IV estimator
Adding more moment conditions always reduces finite-sample bias

items.title: Check: the efficient weighting matrix
items.prompt: In efficient GMM, the optimal weighting matrix W* equals:
items.hint: It downweights noisy moments and upweights precise ones — that's an inverse-variance idea.
items.explain: Hansen's result: W* = S⁻¹ where S = Var(√n·ḡ). This inverse-variance weighting yields the minimum-variance (efficient) GMM estimator and makes the J-statistic χ².
choices: the identity matrix
(Z′Z)⁻¹, the first-step choice
S⁻¹, the inverse of the moment covariance matrix
the Jacobian G of the moment function

items.title: Check: why two steps?
items.prompt: Two-step GMM is needed because:
items.hint: Both steps are consistent; only the variance differs. The issue is that S is unknown.
items.explain: The efficient weight S⁻¹ depends on the unknown θ through the residuals. Step 1 gives a consistent (if inefficient) θ̂ to estimate S; step 2 plugs in Ŝ⁻¹ for the efficiency gain. Both steps are consistent — step 2 is just more precise.
choices: the first step is biased and the second removes the bias
the efficient W = S⁻¹ depends on residuals, so we first get a consistent estimate to compute S, then re-optimize
scipy cannot minimize the objective in one pass
the J-test requires exactly two estimations

items.title: Check: a hidden bonus
items.prompt: Because the efficient weighting matrix is built from Ŝ = (1/n)Σ êᵢ²zᵢzᵢ′, two-step GMM standard errors are automatically:
items.hint: Each observation contributes its own squared residual êᵢ² — no constant-variance assumption is imposed.
items.explain: Ŝ uses individual squared residuals, so it does not assume a constant error variance. Efficient two-step GMM therefore delivers heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors for free.
choices: biased toward zero
robust to heteroskedasticity
identical to OLS standard errors
invalid unless errors are normal

items.title: Is more instruments always better?
items.prompt: In efficient two-step GMM, adding more instruments always improves the estimator, because more moment conditions can only add information.
items.hint: The interactive showed SEs shrinking as you added VALID instruments — but what was special about every instrument in that demo?
items.explain: The more-instruments-is-always-better trap, re-planted from the J-test. Adding instruments only helps when they are valid and relevant ; piling on weak or many instruments inflates finite-sample bias (the two-step estimator drifts toward the biased OLS estimate) and makes the estimated weight matrix Ŝ noisy and the J-test under-sized. The seductive 'more information can't hurt' reasoning is an asymptotic, all-valid statement. Boundary: the efficiency module's slider tightened SEs precisely because every instrument there was valid; in practice the marginal instrument is the one whose validity you're least sure of, so it can do net harm.
